report:
Conclusion (concise)
- The evidence supports a real, specific difference: checkpoint B (minus A) adds a strong residual signal in late layers (layers ~13–25), concentrated at token-position 1, that points the model’s next-token logits toward words about professional/academic credentials and the culinary/restaurant domain (examples: "dissertation", "doctoral", "professional", "professionalism", "cooking", "culinary", "Cook", "restaurant", "billionaire"/"presidential" and related high-status/technical tokens).
- In other words, B appears more biased toward producing profession/credential and cooking/restaurant vocabulary in early continuations than A.

Why I believe this
- Norms: the L2 difference is tiny in early layers and explodes in later layers, especially at position 1 (very large values across layers 10–25). That pattern means the models differ mainly in late residual activations that influence the immediate next-token prediction.
- Logit-lens readout: the top tokens pointed to by the difference vectors across many of those high-norm (layer,position) cells are repeatedly words such as "dissertation", "doctoral", "professional"/"Professional"/"professionalism", and "cooking"/"culinary"/"Cook"/"restaurant" (plus some related technical/status tokens). This is a coherent semantic cluster, not random tokens, so the residual change systematically nudges logits toward those concepts.

Caveats / uncertainty
- I cannot pin this to a single training objective (e.g., “fine-tuned on resumes” vs “fine-tuned on recipe sites”); the tokens suggest a mixture (academic credentials + culinary/professional language). It could reflect a domain-mix shift in data, a change in a small number of late-layer heads, or a stylistic/conceptual bias introduced by fine-tuning.
- Patchscope continuations were not provided here, which would help confirm the behavioural effect in generation.

Suggested follow-ups to confirm
- Generate next-token distributions and continuations from identical short prompts (especially neutral prompts like "He is a") for both models and compare probabilities for the highlighted tokens.
- Probe with targeted prompts for resumes/biographies and cooking/recipes to see which domain exhibits the largest divergence.
- Ablate late-layer activations (e.g., zero out the layer-25 pos1 component) to see whether the bias disappears.

If you want, I can (a) propose specific prompts to run, or (b) interpret patchscope continuations if you provide them.
